transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Romero (Redwood AE), Samir Khan (Redwood SE), Jaya Patel (Argentum - Head of ML), Marco Ruiz (Argentum - Infra), Ellen Cho (Argentum - Finance)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on cost/unit economics for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer has a mid-size quant research org, heavy batching across models for document summarization and reranking. Main asks: per-token pricing at scale, batching & caching levers, dedicated capacity pricing/commit, latency vs cost tradeoffs, and compliance/budget timeline.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and cost pain points
- Typical prompts / seq lengths and QPS
- Batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization options
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private economics & commit models
- Next steps: pricing spreadsheet, POC benchmark, security docs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Romero: Hey everyone, thanks for joining uh this is Alex from Redwood. Samir from our SE team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:04] Jaya Patel: Good thanks, yeah excited to dig in. We kinda... we need to understand cost right away, so appreciate you squeezing this in.
[00:09] Samir Khan: Awesome. Quick intros then we'll jump in. Samir, SE, I focus on perf and deployment.
[00:14] Marco Ruiz: Marco here, infrastructure lead. We're evaluating a few things: hosted for fast time-to-value, dedicated for predictable throughput, and possible private for compliance.
[00:21] Ellen Cho: Ellen - finance. For us the bottom-line is monthly run-rate and whether the committed model moves the needle.
[00:26] Alex Romero: Perfect. Jaya, can you describe your workload and what you mean by "cost"? e.g., embeddings, chat, long sequences?
[00:33] Jaya Patel: Mostly summarization and reranking across alt data, and a multi-step pipeline: chunking -> embed -> rerank -> generate. Sequence lengths: chunking gives ~1k tokens typically, final generate can be 2k-6k depending on prompt. QPS right now low but spikes during close windows - think 50-200 rps in peak events across teams.
[00:51] (slight crosstalk)
[00:53] Samir Khan: OK that helps. So two big levers for cost: per-token price and inference efficiency batching and KV/prefix caching. We usually model savings from batching for throughput workloads and from prefix/KV cache for multi-step pipelines where the same context repeats.
[01:05] Jaya Patel: How significant are those savings in practice? We have a 10M token/month target and that's already, uh, non-trivial.
[01:13] Samir Khan: In our benchmarks, batching can reduce per-token server cost by 20-50% depending on model size and request shape. KV cache can be dramatic for rerank-like workloads: if you can reuse the encoder prefix, you avoid re-running parts of the model which reduces active compute. For summarization with repeated prefixes we see 30-60% token compute reduction.
[01:30] Marco Ruiz: Is that automatic on hosted or do we need to configure?
[01:33] Alex Romero: Hosted includes automatic batching and standard caching heuristics, but you can tune policies. For Dedicated you get more control configure cache TTLs, eviction, and batching targets.
[01:44] Ellen Cho: Pricing  - can you give ballpark per-token numbers? We need ranges to model cash flow.
[01:49] Alex Romero: Sure I'll give ranges with the caveat that I'll send a spreadsheet after. Hosted tier: ballpark $0.0006 to $0.002 per input+output token depending on model size and volume tiers. Dedicated effective unit cost often drops materially under commit think 20-60% lower once you amortize reserved capacity and get lower infra margins. Private depends on customer infra cost plus Redwood support; typically similar to Dedicated at scale but with infra OPEX on your side.
[02:14] Jaya Patel: 0.0006 to 0.002 — that's pretty wide. What's driving the top end? Large seq lengths and small volume?
[02:20] Samir Khan: Exactly. Also choice of model (e.g., 8B vs 70B) and quantization. Larger models and higher seq lengths burn more tokens and memory. For long-context generates (4k-6k) you get both more tokens and more KV cache work; cost per inference goes up linearly with output tokens and sublinearly with cached prefix if reused.
[02:36] Marco Ruiz: Can you walk through an example? We have a 2k input -> 3k output typical run, 100 qps peak, monthly tokens ~15M. What differences would we see hosted vs dedicated?
[02:45] Samir Khan: Back-of-envelope: hosted at $0.0012/token average -> 15M tokens = $18k/mo. With dedicated with a 1-year commit that offsets infra overhead you'd be closer to $9k-$12k/mo depending on instance size and packing. But the tradeoff is you need reserved capacity and commit. Also dedicated has better SLOs for latency.
[03:09] Ellen Cho: So a 30-50% savings, but with a commit. We need to model that vs our procurement cycles.
[03:15] Jaya Patel: How is concurrency handled? Do you lose latency when batching? Our users are latency-sensitive for interactive flows.
[03:21] Samir Khan: There are two modes: latency-first and throughput-first. For interactive we bias toward small batches and lower-latency kernels; that increases per-token marginal cost. Throughput jobs (async bulk) can batch more aggressively. We also have smart routing to send interactive to low-latency pool and background to high-throughput pool.
[03:38] (brief pause)
[03:40] Alex Romero: Another lever is quantization. If you can accept a small accuracy delta, 4-bit quantization on some models can cut memory and cost and increase batching efficiency. That tends to be more relevant for Dedicated/Private where we can run custom kernels.
[03:53] Marco Ruiz: Any examples on accuracy tradeoffs? Our quant research team is sensitive.
[03:57] Samir Khan: Generally for tasks like embeddings and many summarization tasks, LLMs are robust to quant. For instruction-following generation you might see small regeneration differences; we recommend running a small eval set. We'll include recommended quant profiles in the spreadsheet.
[04:12] Jaya Patel: About KV cache — our pipeline reuses document embeddings and partial context across requests. How is cache hit rate estimated?
[04:18] Samir Khan: You provide sample traffic; we run a POC that simulates your workload. Cache hit rates depend on how deterministic the prefixes are and how many unique tokens/prefixes exist. In many enterprise doc workflows we see 40-70% effective reuse.
[04:32] Marco Ruiz: If we go Dedicated, is autoscaling included? We may need burst capacity during earnings days.
[04:38] Alex Romero: Yes Dedicated includes autoscaling policies and burst pools, configurable. Burst is billed differently but cheaper than over-provisioning reserved capacity.
[04:47] Ellen Cho: Security — if some data is sensitive, does hosted store logs? Retention? Is KMS supported?
[04:52] Alex Romero: Hosted provides configurable retention and you can disable logs. We offer KMS/HSM integrations for key management. For strict requirements Private (VPC/on-prem) is best; Dedicated has options for customer-managed keys and audit logs. We'll share SOC 2 and security docs.
[05:07] Jaya Patel: Timeline — our RFP and procurement window is end of Q2. We need numbers for board review in two weeks.
[05:14] Ellen Cho: Right. We'll need a model for run-rate and committed vs on-demand comparisons.
[05:18] Alex Romero: We'll send the detailed spreadsheet with scenarios: hosted pay-as-you-go, dedicated with 6/12/24 month commits, and a private cost estimate. We'll also include sample POC steps to validate latency and cost.
[05:28] (typing noise)
[05:31] Samir Khan: For the POC we typically ask for a representative prompt set, expected QPS distribution, and target latency SLOs. We run a two-week benchmark: one week on hosted to measure baseline, and one week on dedicated/pinned infra to compare.
[05:44] Marco Ruiz: Can Redwood help with running on-prem benchmarks if we want Private estimates?
[05:48] Samir Khan: Yes—our SE team can provide a containerized harness and guidance. For fully air-gapped installs there's more ops work but we have a playbook.
[05:56] Jaya Patel: What about function calling and streaming? Do those affect cost?
[05:59] Alex Romero: Streaming doesn't change token accounting; function calling can increase tokens for the additional system messages, so you should include that in estimates. We can show sample calculations.
[06:08] Ellen Cho: Anything else that materially impacts unit economics we should watch for?
[06:11] Samir Khan: Model selection is huge. Using a smaller model for reranking or embedding and a larger model only for final generation reduces tokens run on big models. Also intelligent routing (route cheap traffic to small models) helps.
[06:21] Alex Romero: We'll also include suggested batching targets and cache TTLs by workload in the spreadsheet.
[06:26] Jaya Patel: Good. For POC success criteria: we want 30-40% cost reduction vs current self-host baseline, maintain 95th latency under 400ms for interactive, and parity on QA for our eval prompts.
[06:38] Samir Khan: That’s reasonable. We'll map metrics to those targets and instrument token-level telemetry.
[06:44] Marco Ruiz: Any minimum commit sizes for Dedicated?
[06:47] Alex Romero: Typical starts at a monthly equivalent of one to two GPU pods depending on model. We'll include examples in the pricing sheet with commitment tiers and projected unit prices.
[06:58] (short silence)
[07:00] Ellen Cho: From a procurement perspective we need a ballpark MSA and pricing to start internal approval.
[07:05] Alex Romero: We'll attach a draft MSA and standard terms; redacted for negotiation but enough for procurement to start.
[07:11] Jaya Patel: Great. Any risks we should call out now?
[07:14] Samir Khan: The usual: model/regression risk if you change model family or quantize aggressively; capacity risk if spikes exceed reserved burst; and perf tuning – sometimes we need to iterate on batching and kernel choices for lowest latency. We mitigate with canary rollouts and fallback policies.
[07:30] Marco Ruiz: How long before we can get numbers?
[07:32] Alex Romero: We'll have the spreadsheet and SOC docs by Friday (2026-03-06). SE number crunch for the specific 2k/3k example will be by Monday (2026-03-09).
[07:41] Ellen Cho: Sounds good. We'll aim to schedule the POC kickoff after we review the sheet.
[07:45] Alex Romero: Perfect. Anything else?
[07:47] Jaya Patel: One quick thing — can you include comparisons against OpenAI/Anthropic for the same traffic? We want apples-to-apples.
[07:53] Alex Romero: Yes we can include competitor cost comps with public pricing assumptions.
[07:57] (wrap up)
[07:58] Alex Romero: Ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck and spreadsheet. Appreciate your time.
[08:03] Marco Ruiz: Thanks.
[08:04] Ellen Cho: Thanks.
[08:05] Jaya Patel: Thanks, bye.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: some words lightly garbled (e.g. "keev cache" instead of KV cache in one auto section), speaker labels may be slightly off in automated export.

Attachments referenced: Pricing spreadsheet (to be sent), SOC2 + security docs (link to be shared), draft MSA (to be attached), POC harness repo (SE to share link).
